# Introduction

Package `gtfs2gps` allows users to convert public transport GTFS data
into a single `data.table` format with GPS-like records, tracking the
space-time position of individual vehicles at high spatial and temporal
resolutions. This GPS-like data format is quite convenient as it can be
easily used in various applications for running transport simulations,
scenario analyses, data visualizations etc.

To start using the package, you can install it from CRAN:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("gtfs2gps")
```

# Loading data

After loading the package, you can read a GTFS feed using `read_gtfs()`.
This function gets a zipped GTFS file and returns a list of `data.table`
objects (a `dt_gtfs` object from {gtfstools}). To demonstrate the package,
we will use a small sample of the GTFS from Porto Alegre, Brazil.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library("gtfs2gps")

# path to gtfs file
gtfs_file <- system.file("extdata/poa.zip", package = "gtfs2gps")

# read gtfs to memory
poa <- gtfs2gps::read_gtfs(gtfs_file)

names(poa)
```

The returning list contains the tables from the GTFS file indexed
according to their file names. `read_gtfs()` checks that the tables
required by {gtfs2gps} are present and not empty:

- `shapes.txt`
- `stop_times.txt`
- `stops.txt`
- `trips.txt`

If the feed has a `frequencies.txt` file, it is used as well.

If you'd like to visualize how the transport network looks like, you can use a few convenient functions from [{gtfstools}](https://github.com/ipea/gtfstools/), our sister package.

```{r poa_shapes_sf, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = has_ggplot}
library(ggplot2)

# get spatial geometries of GTFS
shapes_sf <- gtfstools::get_shapes_geometry(poa)
stops_sf <- gtfstools::get_stops_geometry(poa)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = shapes_sf) +
  geom_sf(data = stops_sf, color = "red", size = .2)
```

Sometimes, GTFS feeds come with internal inconsistencies, for example with trips going too fast, or not accounting for dwell time, etc. We highly recommend that you use {gtfstools} functions to profile, clean and edit your GTFS data before running {gtfs2gps} on it. In the example below, we run `gtfstools::fix_gtfs()`, a simple and convenient function to fix a few of these issues. Here, we use this function to try to cap the max speed between stops at 25 km/h and to set a min dwell time of 30 secs, and the function recalculates the stop times of the feed. Note that `fix_gtfs()` works on the stop times, so some segments of the output of `gtfs2gps()` can still be faster than 25 km/h.

```{r fix_gtfs, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# quick fix
poa_fixed <- gtfstools::fix_gtfs(
  gtfs = poa,
  max_speed = 25,
  min_dwell_time = 30
  )
```


# Converting to GPS-like format

To convert GTFS to GPS-like format, use `gtfs2gps()`. This is the core function of the package. It takes a GTFS zipped file or a GTFS object as an input and returns a `data.table` where each row represents a 'GPS-like' data point for every trip in the GTFS file. In summary, this function interpolates the space-time position of each vehicle in each trip considering the network distance and average speed between stops. The function samples the timestamp of each vehicle every $100m$ by default, but the user can set a different value in the `spatial_resolution` argument. See the example below.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
poa_gps <- gtfs2gps(
  gtfs_data = poa_fixed,
  spatial_resolution = 100
  )
```


### Tip 1: Parallelization

You can use the arguments `parallel = TRUE` and `ncores` to set how
many threads the function can use to parallelize operations. Setting
`ncores` to `4` or `6` can lead to substantial reductions in computation
time in large GTFS feeds.

### Tip 2: Coping with RAM memory limits

In some really large GTFS feeds, the output of `gtfs2gps()`
can sum to dozens of millions of rows. To help with this,
you can pass to the argument `filepath` the path to a local
directory, and the function will save the output of each shape
to a separate file in this directory (`.txt`, or `.rds` with
`compress = TRUE`) without loading them to your RAM.

# Visualizing gtfs2gps output

The output of the `gtfs2gps()` looks like this. Like a traditional
table of a GPS data set, where each row is the timestamp and
location of each vehicle of every trip scheduled in the GTFS.
The output includes a few columns indicating the speed, distance
travelled and whether a given point is at a transit stop.

```{r, message = FALSE}
head(poa_gps)
```

To help with the spatial visualization of the output, you can use 
two support functions to convert the GPS-like data can into `simple feature` 
points or linestrings. Let's see an example with the first 100 data 
points of the sample data we processed, coloured by speed.

```{r, message = FALSE, eval = has_ggplot}
poa_gps100 <- poa_gps[1:100, ]

# points
points_sf <- gtfs2gps::gps_as_sfpoints(poa_gps100)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = points_sf, aes(color = as.numeric(speed))) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "cividis") +
  labs(color = "Speed (km/h)")
```


```{r, message = FALSE, eval = has_ggplot}
# linestring
linestring_sf <- gtfs2gps::gps_as_sflinestring(poa_gps100)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = linestring_sf, aes(color = as.numeric(speed))) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "cividis") +
  labs(color = "Speed (km/h)")

```

Note. the lengh of the trip segments in `gtfs2gps::gps_as_sflinestring()` 
is controlled  with the argument spatial resolition in `gtfs2gps(spatial_resolution = 100)`, which defaults to 100 meters.

# Methodological note

For a given trip, the function `gtfs2gps` calculates the average speed between each pair of consecutive stops given by the ratio between cumulative network distance `S` and departure time `t` for a consecutive pair of valid stop_ids (`i`),

```{r equation, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("https://github.com/ipea/gtfs2gps/blob/master/man/figures/equation1.png?raw=true")
```

Since the beginning of each trip usually starts before the first stop_id, the mean speed cannot be calculated as shown in the previous equation because information on `i` period does not exist. In this case, the function consider the mean speed for the whole trip. It also happens after the last valid stop_id (`N`) of the trips, where info on `i + 1` also does not exist.

```{r speed, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("https://github.com/ipea/gtfs2gps/blob/master/man/figures/speed.PNG?raw=true")
```
